steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our HCI paper on Luminate, a system that uses LLMs to generate and organize a design space of responses so people can explore ideas in human-AI co-creation. Motivate design space thinking, explain what current LLM interaction paradigms miss, introduce our framework and system, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Creativity needs many ideas; fixation; design space thinking
- LLMs as an opportunity, but current interaction paradigms push convergence
- Example: text-to-image systems and unstructured exploration
- Our goal and framework: generate dimensions first, then structured responses
- Luminate and the user study
- Contributions

  - systems generating multiple images focus on prompt refinement to find desired image (cite)
  - no design space for reflection/exploration
  - prompt (e.g. subject) -> set of similar results -> narrow design space
  - Fig. 1 B: alternatives possible, but generation unstructured (no key dimensions/values) and exploration encourages converging, not diverging (cite); see Section 3.2.1
- Goal and framework
  - new interaction paradigm with LLMs that scaffolds design space thinking in human-AI co-creation
  - insights from exploratory search (cite), creativity support (cite), dimensional reasoning (cite), information visualization (cite)
  - explicit enumeration of, visualizing data within, and interaction with principal dimensions -> better understanding/exploration of design space
  - framework (Fig. 1 C): LLM first generates key dimensions for the prompt's topic/task; combine dimensions with prompt to systematically generate responses; users explore via dimensions
- Luminate and study
  - Luminate: interactive system, dimensions first, then responses for structured exploration
  - user study: 14 professional writers in creative writing; potential to help explore design space
- Contributions
  - interaction framework: LLMs should let users explore a space of responses, not a single data point
  - Luminate with novel interaction techniques/features
  - user study: dimensional exploration may prevent fixation and nurture design space thinking

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Linus Pauling, a two-time Nobel prize winner, said: "if you want to have good ideas, you must have lots of ideas and learn to throw away the bad ones". And creative processes do usually begin by generating and exploring many ideas, instead of refining just one. If you don't explore diverse ideas first, you can converge too fast to a sub-optimal idea and spend time iterating on it without thinking about other options, which is called fixation and it hinders creative processes. Apart from helping people avoid fixation, helping them understand the design space, meaning the space of possible ideas and solutions to a task and problem, has been found to be essential in creative processes. So researchers have said that creativity support tools need to support design space thinking, and they have stated various benefits of letting designers use an understanding of the design space in creative processes.

At the same time, large language models (LLMs) today give an unprecedented opportunity to support creative processes. Besides using the generative power of LLMs to automate and speed up creation tasks, they can instantly produce tens to hundreds of outputs, which is especially good for helping users build a comprehensive understanding of the design space. Current user interaction paradigms for LLMs (Fig. 1 A & B) don't fully use this potential. Instead, they help users converge to an idea and refine the prompts (prompt engineering) to get a more polished output from the initial idea or ideas they may have converged to too early.

For example, recent text-to-image generation systems that generate multiple images for exploration focus on helping users refine their prompts to find the image that has the quality or characteristics they want. They do not give a design space for reflection and exploration that would encourage design space thinking. After users add their prompt (e.g., a subject), they quickly get a set of similar results (e.g., images about the subject), which keeps them inside a narrow design space. This approach, shown in Fig. 1 B, does let users explore alternative ideas, but the outputs are generated in an unstructured way (i.e., there is no systematic approach, like structuring the generation of responses by the key dimensions and values that make up the design space), and exploring these outputs encourages users to converge instead of diverge. We explain this argument more in Section 3.2.1.

- Goal and framework
  - new interaction paradigm with LLMs scaffolding design space thinking in human-AI co-creation
  - insights from exploratory search (cite), creativity support (cite), dimensional reasoning (cite), information visualization (cite)
  - enumerating, visualizing, interacting with principal dimensions helps understanding/exploration
  - framework (Fig. 1 C): generate key dimensions first, combine with prompt, systematically generate responses; explore via dimensions
- Luminate and study: dimensions then responses; 14 professional writers; potential to help explore design space
- Contributions: interaction framework (space of responses, not single data point); Luminate; user study (prevent fixation, nurture design space thinking)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Linus Pauling, a two-time Nobel prize winner, said: "if you want to have good ideas, you must have lots of ideas and learn to throw away the bad ones". And creative processes do usually begin by generating and exploring many ideas, instead of refining just one. If you don't explore diverse ideas first, you can converge too fast to a sub-optimal idea and spend time iterating on it without thinking about other options, which is called fixation and it hinders creative processes. Apart from helping people avoid fixation, helping them understand the design space, meaning the space of possible ideas and solutions to a task and problem, has been found to be essential in creative processes. So researchers have said that creativity support tools need to support design space thinking, and they have stated various benefits of letting designers use an understanding of the design space in creative processes.

At the same time, large language models (LLMs) today give an unprecedented opportunity to support creative processes. Besides using the generative power of LLMs to automate and speed up creation tasks, they can instantly produce tens to hundreds of outputs, which is especially good for helping users build a comprehensive understanding of the design space. Current user interaction paradigms for LLMs (Fig. 1 A & B) don't fully use this potential. Instead, they help users converge to an idea and refine the prompts (prompt engineering) to get a more polished output from the initial idea or ideas they may have converged to too early.

For example, recent text-to-image generation systems that generate multiple images for exploration focus on helping users refine their prompts to find the image that has the quality or characteristics they want. They do not give a design space for reflection and exploration that would encourage design space thinking. After users add their prompt (e.g., a subject), they quickly get a set of similar results (e.g., images about the subject), which keeps them inside a narrow design space. This approach, shown in Fig. 1 B, does let users explore alternative ideas, but the outputs are generated in an unstructured way (i.e., there is no systematic approach, like structuring the generation of responses by the key dimensions and values that make up the design space), and exploring these outputs encourages users to converge instead of diverge. We explain this argument more in Section 3.2.1.

So the goal of this work is to explore a new interaction paradigm with LLMs that scaffolds and encourages design space thinking in the human-AI co-creation process. For this, we take insights from previous work in exploratory search, creativity support, dimensional reasoning, and information visualizations. These fields have shown again and again that explicitly enumerating the principal dimensions related to the target domains or tasks, visualizing data within them, and interacting with them can improve understanding and exploration of the design space. Based on this, we propose a human-AI collaboration framework (Fig. 1 C). We don't generate responses directly from the user's prompt. Instead we first prompt LLMs to generate key dimensions related to the topic or task in the original prompt, and then we combine these dimensions with the original prompt to systematically generate responses that build the design space. Then users can use the dimensions to explore the generated design space in a structured and systematic way.

To show that this framework is feasible and useful, we built Luminate, an interactive system that uses LLMs to first generate key dimensions from a user's prompt and then generate responses with these dimensions, for structured exploration of LLM outputs. We did a user study with 14 professional writers who specialize in creative writing, and it shows that our approach has the potential to help users explore the design space effectively in their creative processes. Our work is a step towards making LLMs more interactive and useful for creative processes. Our contributions are:

- A new interaction framework for human-AI collaboration in creative tasks, based on the idea that LLMs should let users explore a space of possible responses instead of giving a single data point as a response to user input.

- Luminate, an interactive system that shows this idea with new interaction techniques and features for structured generation and exploration of LLM outputs.

- A user study that shows that letting users explore the LLM output space by dimensions has the potential to prevent fixation and nurture design space thinking.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
A dictum from Linus Pauling, a two-time Nobel prize winner, states: "if you want to have good ideas, you must have lots of ideas and learn to throw away the bad ones" [1]. Indeed, creative processes typically begin with generating and exploring multiple ideas rather than refining a single one. Without first exploring diverse ideas, one can hastily converge to a sub-optimal idea and spend time iterating on it without considering other options, a phenomenon called fixation that hinders creative processes [2,3,4]. Besides helping people avoid fixation, helping them understand the design space (the space of possible ideas and solutions to a task and problem) has been found to play an essential role in creative processes [5,6,7,8]. Thus, researchers have voiced the need to support design space thinking in creativity support tools, citing various benefits of giving designers the ability to leverage an understanding of the design space in creative processes [9,10,6,11,7,12].

On the other hand, large language models (LLMs) today offer an unprecedented opportunity to empower creative processes. In addition to using LLMs' generative power to automate and accelerate creation tasks [13,14,15], their capacity to instantly produce tens to hundreds of outputs is especially conducive to helping users develop a comprehensive understanding of the design space [12,16], a potential that current user interaction paradigms for LLMs (Fig. 1 A & B) do not fully harness. Instead, current interaction paradigms help users converge to an idea and refine the prompts (prompt engineering) to produce a more polished output from initial idea(s) they may have prematurely converged to.

For example, recent text-to-image generation systems that generate multiple images for exploration focus on helping users refine their prompts to find the image that fits their desired quality or characteristics [17,18]. They do not provide a design space for reflection and exploration that would encourage design space thinking. Instead, after users add their prompt (e.g., subject), they are quickly presented with a set of similar results (e.g., images about the subject), which confines them within a narrow design space. Although this approach, illustrated in Fig. 1 B, allows users to explore alternative ideas, the generation of these outputs is unstructured (i.e., it does not use a systematic approach, such as structuring the generation of responses using key dimensions and values that make up the design space), and the exploration of these outputs encourages users to converge rather than diverge [4], an argument we elaborate on further in Section 3.2.1.

The goal of this work, therefore, is to explore a new interaction paradigm with LLMs that scaffolds and encourages design space thinking in the human-AI co-creation process. To do so, we draw insights from prior work in exploratory search [19,20,21], creativity support [2,22,4], dimensional reasoning [7,23], and information visualizations [24,25]. These fields have repeatedly demonstrated that explicit enumeration of, visualizing data within, and interaction with the principal dimensions associated with the target domains or tasks can enhance understanding and exploration of the design space. Based on these insights, we propose a human-AI collaboration framework (Fig. 1 C). Instead of generating responses directly from the user's prompt, we first prompt LLMs to generate key dimensions associated with the topic or task in the original prompt, and then combine the derived dimensions with the original prompt to systematically generate responses that construct the design space. Users can then use these derived dimensions to explore the generated design space in a structured, systematic manner.

To demonstrate the feasibility and usefulness of this framework, we instantiated it as Luminate, an interactive system that uses LLMs to first generate key dimensions from a user's prompt and then generate responses using these dimensions for structured exploration of LLM outputs. Our user study with 14 professional writers specializing in creative writing shows that our approach has the potential to help users effectively explore the design space during their creative processes. Our work is a step towards improving the interaction and usefulness of LLMs in assisting creative processes. In summary, our contributions include:

- A new interaction framework for human-AI collaboration in creative tasks, built on the premise that LLMs should allow users to explore a space of possible responses rather than giving a single data point in response to user input.

- Luminate, an interactive system that demonstrates this idea with novel interaction techniques and features for structured generation and exploration of LLM outputs.

- A user study demonstrating that enabling dimensional exploration of the LLM output space has the potential to prevent fixation and nurture design space thinking.
